The regional map’s camp symbols are unnamed and are not used to identify the three named sites. This is UNHCR’s retrospective account, including criticism of its own conduct. The underlying interviews and field correspondence, the whole book and the original Global Appeal 1999 overview were not separately consulted. Accessed 15 September 2026.

case_name: Merv: capture, captivity and repeated destruction
displaced: Residents of Merv driven out of the city; selected artisans and children taken into captivity, and survivors exposed to renewed attacks.
settlers: Tolui’s Mongol army and later Mongol commanders and detachments; officials installed after the capture.
source_labels: ʿAla-ad-Din ʿAta-Malik Juvaini, The History of the World-Conqueror, volume I, translated by John Andrew Boyle (1958), chapter XXVII, printed pp. 153–168 (PDF physical pp. 205–220), especially pp. 160–164 and 166–168. The chapter was read in the retained Internet Archive PDF; native pp. 162 and 164 were inspected. The 400 artisans and unspecified children on p. 162 are not identified as the later Bokhara-directed group on p. 164. Reported death totals remain unverified. The original Persian text was not consulted. Accessed 15 September 2026. | Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion (Yale University Press, 2017), printed pp. 169–176 (PDF physical pp. 196–203), especially p. 171 and note 155 on p. 481; notes on pp. 481–482 also consulted. Native p. 171 and map 2, printed p. 94 (PDF p. 121), were inspected. The map labels Merv and Bukhara but does not establish their travel route. Jackson challenges the chroniclers’ population figures; his 10,000 for later killings differs from the hundred thousand in the retained Boyle translation, p. 166. Neither figure is adopted here. Underlying works cited in the notes were not separately consulted. Public link is an unofficial PDF mirror. Accessed 15 September 2026.

case_name: Cambodian refugees forced back at Preah Vihear
displaced: Cambodian refugees rounded up in Thai border camps and forced into Cambodia at Preah Vihear.
settlers: Thai soldiers carrying out the roundup and forced return; the ICRC and UNHCR appear in the protection response, not as settlers.
source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, chapter 4, “Flight from Indochina,” printed p. 92 (PDF p. 14); surrounding Cambodian context on pp. 91–93 (PDF pp. 13–15) and chapter endnotes 1 and 19–24 (PDF p. 26). UNHCR’s retrospective account; figures and its account of its own response are attributed to it. The underlying Robinson, McNamara and Shawcross works and the A/49/12 report mentioned in the inherited source log were not separately consulted. Retained copy consulted 15 September 2026. | Henry Kamm, “Thais Deport 30,000 Cambodians While Others Continue to Arrive,” New York Times report reproduced by Stephen J. Solarz in Congressional Record, Extensions of Remarks, 15 June 1979, printed pp. 15109–15110 (PDF physical pp. 29–30), especially p. 15110 left column. Used only for attributed regional bus-movement context. Original newspaper issue date and underlying interviews were not independently checked; reported totals are not substituted for the accepted UNHCR retrospective. The unnamed assembly place and pass are not located by this source.

case_name: Hmong asylum seekers pushed back to Laos
displaced: Several hundred Hmong reported pushed back from Thailand to Laos in 1986.
settlers: Thai authorities in the border pushback and screening system; UNHCR had an observation and appeal role in screening. The chapter does not identify the units carrying out the reported pushbacks.
source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, chapter 4, “Flight from Indochina,” printed p. 101 (PDF p. 23), with surrounding context on pp. 100–102 and chapter endnotes 1 and 37–39. The 1986 pushback magnitude is attributed to border reports in UNHCR’s retrospective; the underlying reports and Robinson’s book were not separately read.

case_name: Old Urgench: destruction and captive removal
displaced: Residents of Gurganj, or old Urgench, including artisans, children and young women taken captive, and men selected for execution in Juvaini’s account.
settlers: Mongol forces sent by Chinggis Khan under Chaghadai and Ögedei; the sources do not establish the composition of the later city’s resident population.
source_labels: Juvaini, The History of the World-Conqueror, vol. I, translated by J. A. Boyle, chapter XIX, pp. 123–128 (especially p. 123 n. 1 and pp. 127–128). | Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World, pp. 76, 78, 158, 169–171, 173 and 176–177. | ICOMOS, “Kunya-Urgench (Turkmenistan), No 1199,” evaluation appended to the UNESCO World Heritage nomination dossier, printed pp. 72–73 (PDF physical pp. 240–241), especially p. 73, History continuation. Used for the 1221 destruction date and heritage-site context; this modern heritage summary is not casualty evidence or a surveyed 1221 city footprint.

case_name: Compulsory Ujamaa villagization in Tanzania
displaced: Rural Tanzanian households compelled to move into concentrated villages; detailed evidence here concerns Mtwara in the southeast.
settlers: The Tanzanian government and TANU party; in Mtwara, TANU Youth League and People’s Militia members carried out forced resettlement.
source_labels: Priya Lal, “Self-Reliance and the State: The Multiple Meanings of Development in Early Post-Colonial Tanzania,” Africa 82(2), 2012, pp. 212–234, especially pp. 212, 219–225. Detailed local evidence includes the author’s 2008 interviews in Mdui, Rwelu and Nanguruwe; those interviews were read through this article, not independently consulted. | World Bank, Tanzania Agricultural Sector Report, Report 4052-TA, 19 August 1983, printed pp. 142–145, especially §§6.6–6.7 (PDF pp. 161–162). Country and regional orientation: map IBRD 2802R3, “Tanzania—Regions and Districts,” September 1976 (PDF p. 229). Village-residence totals are not treated as forced-mover counts.

case_name: Merina expansion, military colonies and coerced labour
displaced: People subjected to Merina conquest, enslavement and compulsory labour, including Betsileo and Betsimisaraka communities. Merina subjects also owed compulsory service; large parts of Sakalava country remained outside effective Merina rule.
settlers: The Merina monarchy, army, officials and allied elites, including soldiers established in military colonies.
source_labels: Gwyn Campbell, An Economic History of Imperial Madagascar, 1750–1895: The Rise and Fall of an Island Empire, revised French edition translated by Charles-Edouard Bistodeau, Indian Ocean World Centre (translation in progress). Introduction, PDF pp. 6–7 and 10; chapter 3, PDF pp. 9, 11 and 16–17. Geographic orientation: chapter 1, Carte 1 (printed p. 19 / PDF p. 2) and Carte 3 (printed p. 32 / PDF p. 15). These locators refer to the French files, not the original English edition. | Gwyn Campbell, “Unfree labour, slavery and protest in imperial Madagascar,” in Resisting Bondage in Indian Ocean Africa and Asia (2007), chapter 5, pp. 49–59, especially pp. 50–51 and 54–58. Public author-uploaded chapter; historical sources cited within it were not independently consulted.

case_name: Peru internal armed conflict displacement
displaced: Civilians uprooted within Peru, many from rural Indigenous and Quechua-speaking communities in the Andes and central forest.
settlers: Shining Path (PCP-SL), Peruvian security forces, and—in some Amazonian localities—the MRTA; abusive self-defense groups also caused displacement.
source_labels: Comisión de la Verdad y Reconciliación (Peru), Informe final, Tomo VI, §1.9.1, “El desplazamiento interno,” printed pp. 627–658. Definition: p. 629; causes and estimation limits: pp. 634–637; origins, refuges and repeated movement: pp. 640–644; actors and conclusions: pp. 649–656. The commission’s approximately half-million estimate covers 1980–2000 (p. 653). Original report consulted through a retained Derechos/Nizkor mirror; underlying studies and individual testimony files were not independently consulted.

case_name: South Tyrol Option Agreement population transfer
displaced: German- and Ladin-speaking South Tyroleans facing pressure to leave their homeland or remain under Italian assimilation.
settlers: Fascist Italian and Nazi German governments and their resettlement agencies; South Tyrolean emigrants received mainly in Austrian territory then incorporated into the German Reich.
source_labels: Emmanuel Dalle Mulle and Alessandro Ambrosino, “The 1939 Option Agreement and the ‘Consistent Ambivalence’ of Fascist Policies towards Minorities in the Italian New Provinces,” The Historical Journal 66(4) (2023), pp. 887–908, DOI 10.1017/S0018246X23000158. Introduction and sections III, V–VI: assimilation, competing government objectives, declarations versus departures, and incomplete implementation. | Tiroler Landesarchiv, Archivglossar U, entry “Umsiedlung (Südtirol).” Complete entry: resettlement agencies, Innsbruck transit, receiving regions, limits of official totals, and postwar return. Undated web entry; underlying administrative records not independently inspected. | Autonome Provinz Bozen – Südtirol, Abteilung Deutsche Kultur, “Option – Heimat – Opzioni,” project description, undated. Description explicitly includes German-speaking South Tyroleans and Ladins in the coerced choice of 1939–1943; exhibition dates are not a publication date.

case_name: Herat after the revolt: punitive reconquest
displaced: Residents remaining in Herat after the first capture; previously removed weaver households are a separate cohort.
settlers: Mongol punitive forces under Eljigidei, dispatched by Chinggis Khan.
source_labels: Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017), p.159 and p.477 n.48 (two captures, punitive reconquest, enslavement of some women and burning); pp.225–226 (separate weaver removal) and p.177 (later return and recovery). Underlying chronicles not independently consulted. | Maria Szuppe, “Herat iii. History, Medieval Period,” Encyclopaedia Iranica XII/2, pp.206–211 (2003; updated2013), Mongol invasion and initial post-Mongol sections, publisher-generated PDF pp.6–7. Quantitative medieval totals not adopted. | Peter Jackson, “Eljigidei,” Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/4, pp.366–367 (1998; updated2013), first general and bibliography only. Later namesake excluded; million-plus death total rejected as unreliable. | Arash Khazeni, “Herat i. Geography,” Encyclopaedia Iranica XII/2, pp.203–205 (publisher Published field: 2003; updated 2013), town-location and Harirud-valley paragraphs. Modern town reference used for geographic orientation only, not a 1221–1222 event boundary, massacre site or captive route.

case_name: Expulsion of Lhotshampa from Bhutan
displaced: Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa residents of southern Bhutan, including families reclassified as non-nationals, pressured to leave, or fleeing repression.
settlers: Bhutanese citizenship authorities, local administrators and security forces; departure and refuge involved different circumstances for different families.
source_labels: Amnesty International, Bhutan: Human Rights Violations against the Nepali-speaking Population in the South, December 1992, AI Index ASA 14/04/92, printed pp. 1–11. Delegation/interview methods, citizenship and cultural policies, protest and repression, and reported opposition abuses. These selected pages were read; underlying government publications, legislation and interview files were not independently inspected. | Amnesty International, Bhutan: Forcible exile, August 1994, AI Index ASA 14/04/94, printed pp. 1–32. Full textual body consulted; census/departure cases pp. 14–26, government denials and anti-eviction measures pp. 29–32. The 1994 camp stock and 1994 departure examples are outside this case’s 1988–1993 window. | Deepesh Das Shrestha, “El reasentamiento de refugiados butaneses supera las 100.000 personas,” ACNUR/UNHCR, 19 November 2015, Spanish institutional version, translation credited to Ana Ledesma Claros. Complete article consulted for post-2007 resettlement and births during exile only; later camp/resettlement totals are not 1988–1993 displacement estimates.

case_name: Derg resettlement and compulsory villagization in Ethiopia
displaced: Rural residents compelled into planned villages; northern people subjected to interregional resettlement; receiving communities losing land, including Anuak communities in Gambela and the Baro area.
settlers: The Derg government, military and resettlement agencies; incoming northern resettlers included people themselves subjected to coercion.
source_labels: Africa Watch, Evil Days: 30 Years of War and Famine in Ethiopia, September 1991, researched and written by Alex de Waal. Preface and geographical conventions; printed pp. 86–91 (early villagization), 210–226 (resettlement), chapter 13, pp. 229–234 (villagization), and pp. 329–330 (Anuak land loss and integration). Chapters 12–13 read continuously in the publisher’s alternate rendition; exact per-file PDF locators retained. Regional testimony and secondary-source synthesis, not a complete movement register; underlying sources were not all separately read.

case_name: Operation Priboi deportation from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, March-April 1949
displaced: Families designated as kulaks and families of resistance fighters or alleged supporters in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, including children.
settlers: Soviet central and republican security authorities, operational troops and local administrative auxiliaries; the case concerns deported households rather than a separately established replacement-settler population.
source_labels: Pearu Kuusk, “History: 75 years since the post-war mass deportations in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Moldova,” Estonian Internal Security Service, Annual Review 2023–2024, printed pp. 60–61. Original web-extracted PDF text consulted for coordinated March Priboi scope and command structure. Adjacent translated field instructions concern Moldova’s Operation Yug and are not treated as surviving Priboi instructions. | Estonian International Commission for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity, Phase III conclusions on the Soviet occupation from 1944, section 8, printed/PDF p. 9, March 1949 paragraphs. Family removal and collective punishment; adjacent 1945 German and 1951 Jehovah’s Witness deportations are excluded. | International Commission for the Evaluation of the Crimes of the Nazi and Soviet Occupation Regimes in Lithuania, “Deportations of the Population in 1944–1953: Conclusions,” approved 20 April 2005, pp. 1–2, conclusions 3–4 and 7–9. Central 29 January 1949 resolution, local lists, property seizure and collectivization context. Broader-period procedures and totals are not automatically assigned to every Priboi household. | Arvydas Anušauskas, “Gyventojų trėmimai 1944–1953 m.,” Lithuanian commission-hosted study, printed/PDF pp. 10–11, Priboj section and notes 48–56; surrounding pp. 9–12 read to distinguish operations. Lithuanian-language original read; English narrative paraphrase. March removals, documented April follow-up and Bodaibo assignment; alternative figures remain separate reports. Underlying archives cited by the author were not independently inspected. | Museum of the Occupation of Latvia, “A Child from the Underground!”, 25 March 2025, complete article body, especially paragraphs 2–8 on Alma, Alda and Hārdijs Biezais. One family’s March deportation, exile, work and 1956 return, not a representative sample of all destinations or labor conditions; collection objects were not independently examined.

case_name: Ottoman conquest of the Balkans: surgun transfers and Yoruk-Turkmen colonization of Rumelia
displaced: Balkan populations subjected to conquest, removal or compulsory resettlement; Anatolian nomads and other people transferred by the Ottoman state. Experiences and legal status varied.
settlers: Ottoman rulers and frontier authorities; Anatolian Turkish and Yörük settlers, including compulsory transferees and other migrants. People resettled around the capital formed additional, distinct groups.
source_labels: Halil İnalcık, “Ottoman Methods of Conquest,” Studia Islamica 2 (1954), pp. 103–129, especially pp. 122–129, section “Deportation and Emigration as a Tool of Reorganization.” Original article facsimile read. Includes different compulsory and other receiving streams; p. 128 discusses the influx after Timur’s invasion. Chronicles and registers cited by the author were not independently inspected. | Milena Petkova, “The Process of Sedentarization of Semi-nomadic Groups of the Yörüks in Parts of 16th Century Ottoman Rumeli: Migration Control or Tax Control?”, Journal of Balkan and Black Sea Studies 2(3) (December 2019), pp. 25–43; article body pp. 25–37 read, especially pp. 29–37. Original publisher PDF. Regional tax and settlement evidence for Eastern Upper Thrace; not a whole-Rumelia forced-migration count. | Halil İnalcık, “Rumeli,” TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi 35 (Istanbul, 2008), pp. 232–235, especially pp. 232–233. Original Turkish article on the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi website and original print PDF consulted for the 1352 footholds, 1354 capture and geographic terminology. English prose is an author’s paraphrase, not a published translation. This is the same historian as the 1954 article, not independent corroboration of all its claims. | Feridun Emecen, “Gelibolu,” TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi 14 (Istanbul, 1996), pp. 1–6, especially p. 1, the 1352–1376 sequence. Original Turkish article on the TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi website and native PDF p. 1 consulted. Distinguishes the initial foothold, earthquake and capture, settlement, and interrupted possession. English prose is an author’s paraphrase.

case_name: Fiji-bound coerced or deceptively recruited Pacific Island labor removal, October 1864–10 October 1874
displaced: Pacific Islanders taken to Fiji through coercive or deceptive recruitment; the size of this subset within the mixed labor trade is unknown.
settlers: Private recruiters, shipmasters and intermediaries supplying Fiji planters; the British consul and Cakobau government exercised weak pre-Cession regulation.
source_labels: Ralph Shlomowitz, “The Fiji Labor Trade in Comparative Perspective, 1864–1914,” Pacific Studies 9(3) (1986),107–152, especially109–110 and117–118. Original publisher PDF read for recruiting regions, repeat contracts, pre-Cession cotton labor and regulatory failure; whole-trade numbers are not unique coerced-person counts. | Owen W. Parnaby, “The Regulation of Indentured Labour to Fiji,1864–1888,” Journal of the Polynesian Society65(1) (1956),55–66, especially56–61 and notes7,14,36–37. Original journal HTML retrieved through its archived copy. October1864 is the first recruiting departure; arrivals followed later that year. Dated racial judgments are not adopted; cited underlying records were not separately read. | Parliament of the Republic of Fiji, “Our Story,” History of the Parliament, Cession paragraph. Official institutional account gives10October1874; publication date not stated. Used for the political boundary, not for a claim that coercion ended.

case_name: Highveld Difaqane warfare, refuge, and state formation
displaced: Highveld communities subjected to raiding, captive-taking and flight, including women, children and other noncombatants.
settlers: Multiple African political and raiding formations in changing alliances; colonial-frontier traders and settlers were connected to arms, cattle and captive-labor markets. Refuge-seeking newcomers were not all conquerors.
source_labels: Julian Cobbing, “The Mfecane as Alibi: Thoughts on Dithakong and Mbolompo,” Journal of African History 29(3) (1988), 487–519; especially 487–498 and 518–519. Original article retained through CORE. Its causal and missionary-intent claims are contested; its maps are not used as event geometry. | Elizabeth A. Eldredge, “Sources of Conflict in Southern Africa, ca. 1800–1830: The ‘Mfecane’ Reconsidered,” paper for The Mfecane Aftermath colloquium, University of the Witwatersrand, 6–9 September 1991; introduction and printed 23–37, 43–51. Original conference version held by UCT, not silently substituted for a later published version. | Carolyn Hamilton, “The Character and Objects of Chaka: A Re-Consideration of the Making of Shaka as Mfecane ‘Motor’,” Wits African Studies Seminar Paper 294, June 1991; introduction and printed 30–32. This original seminar cover prints “Caroline Hamilton”; the paper is retained and identified separately from the later journal publication.

case_name: Crown and Royal Navy slave-trade interception and Liberated African depot system on St Helena, 1840–1868
displaced: African men, women and children removed from intercepted slave ships and landed on St Helena, including depot residents, those who died, and survivors later settled locally or sent onward.
settlers: British Crown and colonial authorities, the Royal Navy, St Helena’s Vice-Admiralty court, and depot, medical and administrative staff directing reception and survivors’ disposition.
source_labels: Michael D. Bennett, “Slavery in Early St Helena, Part Three: The Consolidation of Slavery, 1695–1730,” Wirebird 52 (2023), conclusion, p. 48. The conclusion dates the later Liberated African depots to 1840–1868; the earlier enslaved-labor colony remains a separate event. | Andrew Pearson, “Dataset to accompany the excavation report for a ‘liberated African’ graveyard in Rupert’s Valley, St Helena, South Atlantic,” Journal of Open Archaeology Data 1:e5 (2012), Context and Spatial/Temporal Coverage. Complete three-page data paper read. Its broad 1840–1872 project label and archaeological sample are not adopted as this event’s endpoint or total deaths. | Andrew Pearson, Distant Freedom: St Helena and the Abolition of the Slave Trade, 1840–1872 (Liverpool University Press, 2016), chapters 4, 6 and 7 and Conclusion: publisher-exposed opening text only. Chapter 6, “After Liberation,” subsection “Colonial labourers,” documents the February 1841 Julia cohort; chapter 7 describes varied local settlement; the Conclusion separates the 1868 final judgment from the 1872 hospital reuse. Full chapters and their underlying archival notes were not read. | Daniel Domingues da Silva, David Eltis, Philip Misevich and Olatunji Ojo, “The Diaspora of Africans Liberated from Slave Ships in the Nineteenth Century,” Journal of African History 55(3) (2014), 347–369, especially p. 348 and pp. 362–363 with note 46. Original article read in the specified passages; not all underlying records. The early-cohort mortality report and wider migration totals have distinct scopes. Some St Helena evidence depends on Pearson and colleagues’ earlier work.

case_name: Australian Stolen Generations child removals
displaced: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children removed from families and communities
settlers: Government and mission authorities, child-welfare institutions and receiving households; this child-removal case does not describe the children as colonizing settlers.
source_labels: Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing them home: National Inquiry into the Separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children from Their Families (1997), Chapter 2, National Overview. Official Australian Human Rights Commission web edition. Underlying testimony and archives are mediated through the inquiry; chapters are one report, not independent corroborating works. | Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing them home: National Inquiry into the Separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children from Their Families (1997), Chapter 3, New South Wales and the ACT. Official Australian Human Rights Commission web edition. Underlying testimony and archives are mediated through the inquiry; chapters are one report, not independent corroborating works. | Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing them home: National Inquiry into the Separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children from Their Families (1997), Chapter 7, Western Australia. Official Australian Human Rights Commission web edition. Underlying testimony and archives are mediated through the inquiry; chapters are one report, not independent corroborating works.

case_name: Greek destruction and Bulgarian exodus from Kukush to the Bulgarian frontier
displaced: Bulgarian civilians of Kukush and Bulgarian villages along the Greek northward line of advance.
settlers: Greek army, including cavalry and infantry detachments, with bashi-bazouk participation under Greek troop protection in some localities.
source_labels: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Report of the International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (Washington, D.C., 1914), chapter II, printed pp. 97–106; Appendix C, nos. 30–38, printed pp. 300–302. Original retained report read in these passages; the main text’s eyewitness attributions and the commission’s inferences are distinguished. Appendix C no. 29 was read for context; no universal order is inferred.

case_name: Cocos (Keeling) estate settlement and controlled labor
displaced: Recruited Malay plantation workers and later generations of the Cocos-Malay community; descendants are not treated as additional arrivals.
settlers: The Clunies-Ross family and estate, within changing British and Australian territorial administration.
source_labels: Parks Australia, Pulu Keeling National Park, History & culture, sections History of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Cocos culture today. Official institutional web history; page publication date unstated. Retained page read for settlement, recruitment, company currency and later changes. | House of Representatives Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, Islands in the Sun: Legal Regimes of Australia’s External Territories and the Jervis Bay Territory (1991), section 4.5.1, printed p. 74. Official PDF’s search-indexed passage read; original PDF download unavailable. The inspected passage concerns Home Island administration after 1955, not a complete labor history. | United Nations, Report of the Special Committee on the Situation with regard to the Implementation of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, A/10023/Rev.1, Volume III (New York, 1977), chapter XVII annex, printed p. 187, paragraph 5(d), (g), (h). Official PDF’s search-indexed passage read; original PDF download unavailable. Proposed reforms are distinguished from implementation.

case_name: Nazi arrests and deportations of Jersey residents to mainland prisons and camps, 1942–1945
displaced: Jersey residents deported under the retaliatory internment order, and separately punished resistance helpers and prohibited-news disseminators
settlers: German occupation, police, prison and camp authorities; Hitler issued the retaliatory order. Jersey authorities protested it. Deportees are not described as incoming colonizing settlers.
source_labels: Jersey Heritage, The German Occupation, undated institutional history webpage; paragraphs on the September 1942 internment order and 1945 repatriation, 1944 resistance-helper arrests, prohibited BBC news and the separate incoming fortification workforce. Retained official HTML read; underlying orders, individual files and camp records not independently inspected.

case_name: Operation Vesna household deportation from Lithuania
displaced: Lithuanian households selected for Operation Vesna, including children; official categories of resistance families, supporters and kulaks are attributed classifications.
settlers: USSR and Lithuanian SSR security and party-administrative authorities, troops and transport personnel; deportees are not labeled colonizing settlers.
source_labels: Lithuanian Special Archives, Šaltas 1948-ųjų pavasaris (Cold Spring of 1948), institutional exhibition introduction and captions: operation timing; echelon 97912 telegram, 15 June 1948, LYA f. V-11, ap. 1, b. 1, l. 109; family handover certificate, 22 May 1948, LYA f. V-5, ap. 1, b. 11126, l. 10. Lithuanian editorial text and captions read; linked Russian archival scans not independently transcribed. | International Commission for the Evaluation of the Crimes of the Nazi and Soviet Occupation Regimes in Lithuania, Deportations of the Population in 1944–1953: Conclusions, approved 20 April 2005, printed pp. 1–3, especially conclusions 3–4, 7–10 and 12–13. Retained original English PDF read; its wider-period totals and general procedures are not Vesna-only measurements.

case_name: Northern Hoa flight from Viet Nam to China
displaced: Hoa and other ethnic Chinese residents of northern Viet Nam who fled overland to China
settlers: Vietnamese authorities implementing expropriation and hostile policies; Chinese authorities providing asylum and settlement, assisted by UNHCR. Refugees are not characterized as colonizing settlers.
source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, chapter 4, “Flight from Indochina,” printed p. 82 (PDF p. 4); context on pp. 79 and 81–83; chapter endnotes 1 and 6 (PDF p. 26). Retained original chapter read for the northern China branch; UNHCR’s retrospective account, not individual crossing records. The underlying Robinson book and A/35/12 report were not independently read.

case_name: LTTE expulsion of Muslims from northern Sri Lanka
displaced: Muslim residents expelled from northern Sri Lankan districts
settlers: Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the expelling organization; no incoming settler cohort is established here
source_labels: Human Rights Watch, Playing the “Communal Card”: Communal Violence and Human Rights (1995), Sri Lanka section, “Indo-Sri Lanka Accord of 1987,” paragraphs on the October 1990 northern Muslim expulsion and continuing displacement, through the section’s conclusion. Original institutional HTML read and retained. The coastal movement estimate and later September 1992 stock are not a harmonized count of this event.

case_name: Karelian evacuation, return and renewed displacement
displaced: Karelian residents evacuated from territories ceded by Finland to the Soviet Union
settlers: Soviet military and territorial pressure; Finnish evacuation and resettlement authorities. Evacuees are not thereby characterized as colonizing settlers.
source_labels: Elina Karila, “Leaving for a new beginning,” Kamera 12/2015, Finnish Heritage Agency English web edition. Complete article and captions read: evacuation/return paragraphs; local Kurkijoki example; postwar settlement paragraphs and 1947 Mellilä caption. An institutional photo essay, not a household register or legal return instrument. Photographs are not reproduced.

case_name: Ethiopian expulsion of Eritrean-designated civilians
displaced: Civilians whom Ethiopian authorities designated Eritrean or of Eritrean origin, including mixed families
settlers: Ethiopian government, police, security services and local authorities; no incoming settler cohort established
source_labels: Human Rights Watch, The Horn of Africa War: Mass Expulsions and the Nationality Issue (29 January 2003), section IV, “Expulsions by Ethiopia,” including overview, citizenship claims, property, detention, urban/rural removals and family-reunification pressure; section III for the peace-agreement boundary. Complete relevant section read in retained original HTML-derived text. Post-agreement movements and broad report totals are not adopted as this event’s impact.

case_name: Eritrean internment and expulsion of Ethiopian residents
displaced: Ethiopian citizens and long-term Ethiopian residents in Eritrea, including Tigrayan workers, civilian internees, women and children
settlers: Eritrean government, security forces, police and internment authorities; private attackers in documented incidents. These actors are not thereby described as incoming settlers.
source_labels: Human Rights Watch, The Horn of Africa War: Mass Expulsions and the Nationality Issue (29 January 2003), section V, “Expulsions by Eritrea”: official policy, early departures, internment, attacks and July–August 2000 expulsions; war/peace boundary context and notes 129–133. Complete section V read, including later movements excluded here. HRW conveys government statements, interviews, press reports and ICRC confirmations; their underlying documents were not independently reread.

case_name: Forced Muslim exodus from Strumnitsa
displaced: Muslim inhabitants of Strumnitsa town and nearby villages removed under the Greek military order
settlers: Greek military authorities carrying out the expulsion; no incoming settler cohort is established for this case
source_labels: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Report of the International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (Washington, D.C., 1914), chapter II, printed pp. 106–108; Appendix A, nos. 3–4, printed p. 278. Appendix D, no. 65, pp. 324–325, read for source-chain and date limits, not as a new event death count. Commission observation, mediated testimony and interpretation are distinguished; the broader Salonica refugee estimate is not adopted as this event’s impact.

case_name: Mongol retaliatory destruction of Bamiyan
displaced: Residents of the besieged fortified city of Bamiyan
settlers: Chinggis Khan and Mongol forces carrying out the siege and retaliation; no incoming settler population is established for this event.
source_labels: ʿAla-ad-Din ʿAta-Malik Juvaini, The History of the World-Conqueror, volume I, translated by John Andrew Boyle (1958), printed pp. 132–133. Retained PDF pages visually read; account dates the event 618/1221–22. Universal killing and no-habitation statements are attributed to the chronicler, not treated as population counts. Persian original not independently read. | Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion (Yale University Press, 2017), printed p. 158. Retained PDF page visually read for retaliation after Möetügen’s death and the report of continuing ruin in Hamd-Allah Mustawfi’s day. The underlying medieval works cited there were not independently read beyond the separately cited Juvaini passage. Public URL is a PDF mirror.

case_name: Deportation of German-origin residents from Estonia
displaced: People of German origin removed from Estonia in the 15 August 1945 action
settlers: Soviet authorities carrying out the deportation; no incoming settler cohort is established for this case
source_labels: Estonian International Commission for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity, conclusions on the second Soviet occupation from 1944 (report published 2008), section 8, printed pp. 8–9, especially the 15 August 1945 paragraph on p. 9. The reported minimum and collective-punishment characterization are attributed to the Commission; underlying research papers and individual archival files were not independently inspected.

case_name: Deportation of German residents from Lithuania
displaced: German residents of Lithuania deported in the 1945 nationality-based action
settlers: Soviet authorities directing and carrying out the deportation; no incoming settler cohort is established for this case
source_labels: International Commission for the Evaluation of the Crimes of the Nazi and Soviet Occupation Regimes in Lithuania, Deportations of the Population in 1944–1953: Conclusions (approved 20 April 2005), conclusion 2, printed p. 1. Complete three-page document read; conclusions 3–5 and 12–15 checked to distinguish the separate German-resident cohort from broader Lithuanian deportation, labor and return accounts. Original p. 1 visually inspected. The Commission’s reported 1,048 is attributed, not adopted as a structured impact estimate. The underlying research report, individual transport lists and Soviet directives were not independently read.

case_name: Obstruction of Jewish return to Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa
displaced: Jewish households whose return to Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa was obstructed or whose renewed departure followed local exclusion
settlers: Local actors obstructing Jewish return; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established for this case
source_labels: Eyal Ginio, “From Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa to Svilengrad: The Ethnic Homogenization of a Thracian Town in the Balkan Wars,” International Journal of Middle East Studies 55(2), 2023, pp. 275–298, especially pp. 293–297. Those five pages were read in the retained publisher PDF; printed p. 294 was visually checked. Contemporary press and communal correspondence are mediated through Ginio; their originals were not independently read. Local exclusion is distinguished from central protective policy and from the separate Uzun Köprü episode.

case_name: Soviet deportation of Koreans from the Far East
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Soviet Koreans collectively removed from the Far East in the 1937 operation
settlers: The Soviet government and NKVD directing compulsory removal and resettlement; the arriving deportees are not thereby identified as voluntary colonizers
source_labels: J. Otto Pohl, “Stalin’s genocide against the ‘Repressed Peoples’,” Journal of Genocide Research 2(2) (2000), printed pp. 277–279. These three original pages were read textually and visually. The account supplies the two 1937 orders, reported removals and receiving conditions; its 1937–1938 mortality estimate is explicitly attributed to Michael Rywkin. Underlying decrees, administrative records, letters and Rywkin’s original study were not independently read.

case_name: Killing and displacement at Boulgar-Keui and Pichman-Keui
displaced: Bulgarian residents of Boulgar-Keui and Pichman-Keui, including survivors displaced during the July 1913 offensive
settlers: Ottoman military authorities and troops; some testimony alleges Greek participation in particular acts, without establishing a distinct incoming settler cohort
source_labels: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Report of the International Commission to Inquire into the Causes and Conduct of the Balkan Wars (1914), printed pp. 130–133. All four pages were read in the retained report; pp. 130 and 133 were visually inspected during authoring. Refugee depositions and Greek documents are mediated through the Commission; their underlying originals were not separately read. The two-village account is kept distinct from the report’s wider eastern-Thrace examples and refugee figures.

case_name: Soviet deportation of Meskhetian Turks and other Muslim communities from Georgia
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Meskhetian Turks, Kurds, Khemshils and other Muslim communities removed from southern Georgia in November 1944
settlers: The Soviet government, NKVD and NKGB directing compulsory removal and resettlement; the arriving deportees are not thereby identified as voluntary colonizers
source_labels: J. Otto Pohl, “Stalin’s genocide against the ‘Repressed Peoples’,” Journal of Genocide Research 2(2) (2000), printed pp. 286–287, especially the final paragraph of p. 286 and its continuation, mortality discussion and Table 5 on p. 287. Both pages were read textually and visually. The original Soviet records cited by Pohl and the frozen Jeremy Smith chapter were not independently read. Pohl’s return-status observation refers to his 2000 publication context.

case_name: Deportation of the Balkars and authorization to return
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Balkars removed from Kabardino-Balkaria in the March 1944 operation and living under the subsequent exile regime
settlers: Soviet authorities directing deportation and later restoration; no distinct voluntary incoming settler cohort is established here
source_labels: J. Otto Pohl, “Stalin’s genocide against the ‘Repressed Peoples’,” Journal of Genocide Research 2(2) (2000), printed pp. 284–285 (PDF pp. 18–19). Both pages were read textually and visually. The Balkar operation and transit report are distinguished from mixed North Caucasian housing and mortality figures. Pohl’s underlying archival records and cited authorities were not independently read. | Helsinki Watch, “Punished Peoples” of the Soviet Union: The Continuing Legacy of Stalin’s Deportations (1991), printed pp. 73–74 (PDF pp. 69–70). Both pages were read textually and visually. Population estimates, reported transit deaths and the January 1957 restoration decree have distinct scopes. Conquest, Nekrich and Tolz are mediated through the report; Khutuev’s interview is read through its published account, not independently verified.

case_name: Operation Ring: expulsion from Armenian villages
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Armenian civilian communities within the bounded Shahumyan/Geranboi and Chaikent/Getashen Operation Ring referent
settlers: Azerbaijani SSR OMON and USSR forces as described by the Court and Human Rights Watch; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established here
source_labels: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, Sargsyan v. Azerbaijan, application no. 40167/06, judgment of 16 June 2015, paragraphs 29–34, especially paragraph 32, printed p. 8 (physical PDF p. 10). Paragraph 32 supplies an attributed historical background account of April–May 1991. Printed pp. 5–9 were read for boundaries; p. 8 was visually inspected. The applicant’s 1992 displacement and later property proceedings are distinct. The sources behind the background account were not independently read. | Human Rights Watch/Helsinki, Azerbaijan: Seven Years of Conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh (December 1994), printed pp. 5–6 and 98–100 (physical PDF pp. 23–24 and 116–118), especially pp. 5 and 99. These retained report passages were read. The report’s spring–summer description, official explanations, reported civilian expulsions and later partial returns are distinguished; broad refugee stocks and the June 1992 counteroffensive are excluded from the bounded 1991 case. Underlying interviews and individual records were not independently authenticated.

case_name: Post-liberation expulsion and residency pressure against Palestinians in Kuwait
displaced: Palestinians still present in Kuwait after 26 February 1991 who were expelled or pressured to depart, including long-term residents and affected families
settlers: Restored Kuwaiti authorities, security forces, government employers and residency authorities; no distinct incoming settler population is established by this account
source_labels: Middle East Watch, “Kuwait,” Human Rights Watch World Report 1992, “Human Rights Developments Since Liberation,” especially the opening chronology, post-liberation killings, administrative expulsions, employment termination, Foreign Residents Re-registration and the separate occupation-era departures. Retained HTML body; source preparation read the substantive section and inspected its notes. This author checked the cited passages in the retained text. Underlying interviews, press accounts, legal records and the separate Nowhere to Go report were not independently read.

case_name: Post-surrender violence and dispossession of Biharis in Bangladesh
displaced: Bihari and other Urdu-speaking non-Bengali residents targeted after the Pakistani surrender; later transfers and refugee returns are distinct movements.
settlers: People involved in anti-Bihari retaliation and property seizure; later Bangladesh and Pakistan authorities shaped citizenship and transfer options. No complete perpetrator roster or distinct incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: UNHCR, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000, chapter 3, “Rupture in South Asia,” printed pp. 73–74 and 76 (PDF pp. 14–15 and 17), especially “The Biharis in Bangladesh.” These pages were read textually and visually; preceding return context on printed p. 71 was read textually. A retrospective institutional account: underlying agreements and citizenship materials were not separately examined. The separate ICJ report in the frozen composite citation was not read and supplies no claim here.

case_name: Anti-Greek pogrom in Istanbul
displaced: Greek residents of Istanbul targeted by violence and destruction; later departures are reported without a complete roster
settlers: Organized rioters and looters; police nonintervention or encouragement is reported, with government involvement in the bombing pretext attributed to a later court finding; no distinct incoming settler cohort established
source_labels: Helsinki Watch, Denying Human Rights and Ethnic Identity: The Greeks of Turkey (1992), Background, printed pp.8–10 (PDF pp.12–14), including notes7–10; printed pp.7 and11 read for boundaries. Decisive pages visually and textually read in the retained report. Consular observations, court findings and figures are mediated through this report; underlying archives, judgment and casualty memo were not independently read.

case_name: Deportation of the Karachays and the difficult return from exile
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Karachays deported from the Karachay Autonomous Oblast in November 1943 and living through exile and the subsequent return process
settlers: Soviet authorities directing deportation, exile and rehabilitation; the Karachay deportee cohort, with no separate voluntary incoming settler population established here
source_labels: J. Otto Pohl, “Stalin’s genocide against the ‘Repressed Peoples’,” Journal of Genocide Research 2(2) (2000), printed pp. 284–285 (PDF pp. 18–19), read textually and visually. The Karachay operation and early food shortages are distinguished from Balkar and mixed North Caucasian mortality. Underlying archival documents and cited authorities were not independently read. | Helsinki Watch, “Punished Peoples” of the Soviet Union: The Continuing Legacy of Stalin’s Deportations (1991), printed pp. 65–67 (PDF pp. 63–65), read textually and visually. The 1939 population, deportation, rehabilitation and 1991 interview have distinct scopes. Conquest, Sheehy and Nekrich are mediated through the report; the decree original and Chomaev’s testimony were not independently verified.

case_name: Expulsion of Greek citizens from Istanbul and restrictions on their assets
displaced: Greek citizens living in Istanbul who were expelled or denied residence renewal; Turkish citizens of Greek descent who departed under pressure are a distinct associated group
settlers: Turkish government and authorities directing expulsion, residence permits and asset restrictions; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established here
source_labels: Helsinki Watch, Denying Human Rights and Ethnic Identity: The Greeks of Turkey (1992), printed pp. 10–11 (PDF pp. 14–15), including footnotes 11–12. Both pages read textually and visually. Expulsion stages, citizenship groups and asset measures remain distinct. Alexandris, Bahcheli, newspaper reports and decree originals are mediated through this report and were not independently read. Adjacent 1955 violence is excluded.

case_name: Drainage and forced displacement of Iraq's Marsh Arabs
displaced: Marsh Arab communities of southeastern Iraq whose subsistence and homes were undermined by government policies
settlers: Iraqi government authorities responsible for repression and water diversion; no distinct incoming settler population established by the cited passage
source_labels: Human Rights Watch, Iraqi Refugees, Asylum Seekers, and Displaced Persons: Current Conditions and Concerns in the Event of War (2003), section II.B, southern-Iraq paragraph and note34; surrounding section II read for boundaries in retained text. Fawcett and Tanner (October2002), p.33, is cited by HRW but not independently read. Pre-invasion reporting; population figures are reported displacement stocks, not adopted event-impact totals.

case_name: Palestinian flight from Kuwait during Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions, 1990–1991
displaced: Palestinian residents of Kuwait who left during Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions; the report does not provide a complete person-level or legal-status roster
settlers: Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions drove the movement described here; the restored Kuwaiti government enters the account only through later non-readmission and absentee-property measures. No distinct incoming settler cohort is established.
source_labels: Middle East Watch, ‘Kuwait,’ Human Rights Watch World Report 1992, ‘Human Rights Developments Since Liberation,’ especially the occupation/war-leaver paragraph (retained HTML line 158; retained text line 67) and reentry confirmation (HTML line 282; text line 129). Only this retained World Report section was read. The separately named Nowhere to Go report in the existing compound work identity is unretained and unread. The roughly 180,000 figure remains attributed prose, later non-readmission is an outcome rather than a second movement, and the post-liberation sibling count is not combined.

case_name: Soviet deportation and confinement of Volga Germans
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Volga Germans forcibly removed from the Volga region; broader Soviet-German deportation and labor-army populations remain separately described
settlers: Soviet government and NKVD authorities directing deportation, special settlement and compulsory labor; the sources do not establish a bounded incoming replacement-settler cohort
source_labels: J. Otto Pohl, “Stalin’s genocide against the ‘Repressed Peoples’,” Journal of Genocide Research 2(2) (2000), printed pp. 279–281 (PDF pp. 13–15). All three pages were read textually and visually. Volga-operation figures are kept separate from broader Soviet-German special-settlement and labor-army stocks; mortality evidence is explicitly incomplete and contradictory. Pohl’s underlying Soviet orders, administrative records and cited studies were not independently read. | Helsinki Watch, “Punished Peoples” of the Soviet Union: The Continuing Legacy of Stalin’s Deportations (1991), Germans section, printed pp. 11–14 (PDF pp. 15–18). All four pages were read textually and visually. The deportation, wider Soviet-German cohorts, forced-labor stage, 1955 surveillance release and later rehabilitation measures remain distinct. Underlying decrees and cited works were not independently read.

case_name: Anfal campaign against Iraqi Kurds
displaced: Kurdish rural communities and Assyrian and other minorities captured or forcibly relocated during the eight Anfal operations; the source does not establish a complete person-level roster
settlers: The Iraqi Ba'athist state, army and security services carried out the campaign. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Middle East Watch, Genocide in Iraq: The Anfal Campaign Against the Kurds (Human Rights Watch, 1993), Introduction, especially printed pp.3–6, 10–16 and 18–19 (physical PDF pp.30–33, 37–43 and 45–46; retained introduction text lines 10–95, 117–141, 285–410, 459–466, 487–510 and 575–629). The eight Anfal operations, 23 February–6 September 1988, remain distinct from the 29 March 1987–23 April 1989 special-powers frame. Halabja is broader genocide context but not technically an Anfal operation, and its deaths are excluded. All reported quantities remain separate and no deduplicated denominator or structured impact is adopted.

case_name: Mogadishu public-land and settlement evictions and relocation pressure, 2012-2013
displaced: Internally displaced people and urban poor removed from Mogadishu public buildings, public land, or private property. Displaced families living in informal settlements appear only in the unproven 2013 relocation plan; no complete household roster is available
settlers: Somali government authorities reclaiming public property and private owners reclaiming property. The report generally identifies some returning refugees and diaspora members among owner-evictors but supplies no person-level flight-history crosswalk and does not establish that every owner was a returnee.
source_labels: Bryld, Kamau and Sinigallia, Analysis of Displacement in Somalia (World Bank Group, 2014), physical PDF p. 17 (printed p. 14) and physical PDF p. 21 (printed p. 18). The 2012 public-building summary evictions are documented as implemented; the 2013 relocation announcement is used only as evidence of planned pressure. No implemented-removal total, roster, destination outcome, unique-person crosswalk, or evictor-to-refugee-history link is inferred.

case_name: South Sudan civil war and mass displacement
displaced: South Sudanese civilians repeatedly displaced within the country or across borders during the 2013–2018 civil-war window; no complete or deduplicated person-level roster is established
settlers: South Sudanese government and opposition forces drove displacement. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Tankink, Belay, Mukasa, Nieuwe Weme, Burman, and Ventevogel, Culture, context and mental health and psychosocial well-being of refugees and internally displaced persons from South Sudan (UNHCR, 2023), physical PDF pp.15–16 and 29–31. The case is bounded to 2013–2018. The December 2013–April 2018 mortality estimates remain nested and separate from displacement; 2021–2022 IDP/refugee stocks are later context only. No quantity is adopted as a deduplicated event total or structured impact.

case_name: Late-April 1994 Karabakh Armenian front-line displacement
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Azerbaijani civilians making a first departure from the named front-line tract because of the late-April 1994 offensive; the reported approximately 50,000 flow overlaps earlier displacement and is not a complete person or household roster
settlers: Karabakh Armenian forces conducted the offensive, with support from Republic of Armenia forces as reported by Human Rights Watch. No incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Human Rights Watch/Helsinki, Azerbaijan: Seven Years of Conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh (1994), printed pp.85-86 and 99-101 (physical PDF pp.107-108 and 121-123), especially printed pp.85 and 100 and footnote 212; retained extraction lines 3087-3102 and 3509-3584. The late-April 1994 Agdam-Barda/Terter/Geranboi front is isolated from the report's 1993, Operation Ring, 1992 and aggregate displacement accounts. The approximately 50,000 report is overlapping and nonunique. Only this Human Rights Watch report was used for this case.

case_name: Somalia state-collapse and inter- and intra-clan conflict displacement, 1991-1995
displaced: Somali civilians internally displaced during the 1991–1995 state-collapse and inter-/intra-clan conflict wave; no complete or deduplicated person-level roster is established
settlers: Armed clan factions and militias drove conflict and displacement. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Bryld, Kamau, and Sinigallia, Analysis of Displacement in Somalia (World Bank Group, 2014), physical PDF pp.13–16 (printed pp.10–13), especially physical pp.14–15. The case is bounded to the report’s 1991–1995 state-collapse and inter-/intra-clan conflict wave. Approximately two million internally displaced at the 1992 height is a peak stock, not an additive flow or unique-person event total; drought/famine and later waves remain separate.

case_name: Second Congo War internal displacement in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, August 1998–June 2003
displaced: Congolese civilians internally displaced by fighting, insecurity, attacks and coercive territorial or resource control during August 1998–30 June 2003; no complete or deduplicated person-level roster is established
settlers: Congolese and foreign state forces, rebel movements and irregular armed groups drove or participated in the conflict. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Democratic Republic of the Congo, 1993–2003: Report of the Mapping Exercise (August 2010), physical PDF pp.19–20 (printed pp.9–10), paragraphs 19–21, and physical PDF pp.362–365 (printed pp.352–355), paragraphs 733–743. The case is limited to August 1998–30 June 2003. Displacement descriptions are not converted into a nonduplicated event total, and conflict deaths remain separate from displacement. Only this OHCHR report was used for this case.

case_name: Japanese occupation-government forced repatriation and depopulation of Hong Kong, December 1941–August 1945
displaced: Hong Kong residents induced or compelled to leave during Japanese occupation, including people arrested or denied secure residence status; voluntary, induced and forced shares are unresolved
settlers: Japanese occupation authorities, military police and administrative bodies implemented population-reduction measures. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Academy of Chinese Studies, “Forced Repatriation,” complete web body, main narrative paragraphs 1–4 and captions on the Repatriation Office, inducements, residence controls, Beaufort Island, 19 May 1942 and December 1944. The case is limited to occupied Hong Kong, December 1941–August 1945. Approximate population figures and incident reports are not combined into an exact forced-removal or death total. Only this Academy page is displayed for this case.

case_name: August 2008 South Ossetia war, conflict flight, and post-ceasefire forced displacement and destruction
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Civilians who fled from areas in and near South Ossetia, including people who fled danger and insecurity and ethnic Georgians subjected to documented forced displacement. Reported flight and non-return quantities remain distinct and nonadditive.
settlers: Georgian, Russian and South Ossetian forces and irregular armed groups drove conflict and coercion. No distinct incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia, Report, Volume I (September 2009), printed pp.10–11, paragraphs 2–3, and printed pp.26–28, paragraphs 25–28 (physical PDF pp.27–29 for the latter). Hostilities are bounded to 7/8–12 August 2008 and immediate post-ceasefire coercion within 2008. The reported approximately 135,000 who fled and more than 35,000 not expected to return soon are not added or treated as unique-person totals. Only this IIFFMCG volume was used for this case.

case_name: Pakistani army and auxiliary violence and displacement in East Pakistan, March–December 1971
displaced: Bengali civilians in East Pakistan, especially Hindus, Awami League supporters, students, and residents of attacked towns and villages; refugees who fled to India. Refugee, internal-displacement, and death figures remain distinct and nonadditive.
settlers: The Pakistani army and associated auxiliary forces were the principal coercive agents. No distinct incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: International Commission of Jurists, The Events in East Pakistan, 1971 (1972), printed and physical PDF pp.37–38 and 50–51. The case is bounded to the Pakistani campaign from 25 March through surrender at Dhaka on 16 December 1971. Refugee, internal-displacement, and death evidence remains distinct; no reported figure is converted into a unique or additive forced-removal total. Only this ICJ report is displayed for this case; UNHCR chapter 3 was used as supporting packet evidence.

case_name: Coordinated Soviet deportation from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, 13-14 June 1941
displaced: People in Soviet-occupied Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania classified by Soviet authorities as anti-Soviet, criminal or socially dangerous and specified family members removed in the coordinated 13–14 June 1941 operation; no complete or deduplicated tri-state person roster is established
settlers: USSR and republican security organs, operational groups and participating local officials carried out the removals. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Latvian State Archive, ‘Deportation of June 14, 1941,’ operation-planning, 13–14 June, family-separation, property and differing-count paragraphs; related Serov instructions, sections 1, 3–5 and 7; Estonian International Commission, Phase III conclusions, section 8, printed p. 8. Latvia and Estonia figures retain their country and cohort definitions; no Lithuania or combined tri-state count, complete destination distribution or forced-labor assignment is inferred. The existing Latvian State Archive operation-account identity is reused for this case.

case_name: Waikato invasions of Taranaki and forced southward movement, 1826–1834
displaced: Taranaki tribal groups that Te Ara says were forced south by the 1826 invasion; Te Āti Awa communities and Taranaki defenders in the later named pā sequence. The source gives no complete identity list, destination roster or population total.
settlers: Waikato forces, including war parties led by Te Wherowhero in the 1830s. The approved source does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this event unit.
source_labels: Basil Keane, ‘Musket wars – Waikato,’ Te Ara – the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, page 4, ‘Hawke’s Bay and Taranaki’ and ‘1830s wars’: the 1826 Waikato invasion and forced movement south, the 1831–32 capture of Pukerangiora, later Taranaki pā fighting and the 1834 Te Ruaki attack. The source gives no generalized removed, casualty or captive total. Existing identity reused without resolving the recorded 2012/2017 story-date discrepancy.

case_name: Detention and forced return of the 158 recognized Nong Khai Lao Hmong refugees, 17 November 2006–28 December 2009
displaced: The recognized Nong Khai Lao Hmong refugee cohort: originally 147 people, increasing to 158 through births during detention. The figures are successive, not additive; children are members of the 158-person cohort, and the 158 are nested within the wider roughly 4,000-person two-site return.
settlers: Thai immigration, security and government authorities carried out the roundup, detention and return; the Lao People's Democratic Republic was the receiving state. No incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: UNHCR, ‘Thailand: UNHCR calls for end of three-year detention of Lao Hmong’ (17 November 2009), first four body paragraphs. UNHCR’s 29 December follow-up was used internally for the terminal 28 December return and access request. The 147 and 158 figures describe the same cohort before and after births in detention; the 158 are nested within, and not added to, the wider roughly 4,000-person two-site return.

case_name: HVO/Herceg-Bosna program against Bosnian Muslims
displaced: Bosnian Muslim civilians and detainees affected by the HZ(R) H-B/HVO program in claimed territory. The approved synthesis gives no nonduplicative program-wide victim total or complete locality roster.
settlers: Political and military leaders of HZ(R) H-B, HVO forces and apparatus, the accused members of the JCE, and certain Croatian leaders as found by the Trial Chamber. This field records responsible actors, not an inferred incoming settler population.
source_labels: ICTY, Prosecutor v. Prlić et al., Trial Judgment, volume IV, paras. 41–45, 65–68, printed pp. 15–16, 23–24 (29 May 2013). The Trial Chamber synthesis supports the no-earlier-than-mid-January 1993 boundary, staged HVO/Herceg-Bosna program, actor structure and integrated removal system through April 1994. It does not supply a nonduplicative program-wide victim total or complete locality roster.

case_name: Mogadishu-centered conflict displacement, 2005-2009
displaced: Mogadishu residents and other civilians affected by repeated waves of conflict displacement. About 300,000 leaving in two months in 2007 is a movement figure; about one million affected by end-2009 is a separate affected-population figure. The measures are nonadditive, nonunique, and do not establish nonrepeated movement.
settlers: The approved pages establish fighting and insecurity as displacement drivers but do not supply a specific event-wide combatant or command roster. No incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: Bryld, Kamau and Sinigallia, Analysis of Displacement in Somalia (World Bank Group, 2014), physical PDF p.14 (printed p.11) for the 2005–2009 boundary and figures, p.15 (printed p.12) for general mechanisms, and p.20 (printed p.17) for later context only. About 300,000 leaving in two months in 2007 is a movement figure; about one million affected by end-2009 is a separate affected-population figure. They are nonadditive and nonunique. December 2013 and April 2014 figures are excluded.

case_name: SAO Krajina/RSK removal of Croats and other non-Serbs
displaced: Croats and other non-Serb residents removed from SAO Krajina and later RSK-controlled territory in Croatia. No complete nonduplicative victim total is claimed.
settlers: SAO Krajina and later RSK leadership, government, MUP/police and Territorial Defence forces, with JNA cooperation as identified by the Trial Chamber. This field records responsible actors, not an inferred incoming settler population.
source_labels: ICTY, Prosecutor v. Milan Martić, Trial Judgment, paras. 129, 132, 151, 442–446, 450–453, printed pp. 44–45, 54, 158–163 (12 June 2007). These passages support the Croatian SAO Krajina/RSK institutional sequence, August 1991 onset, removal purpose and distinct coercive mechanisms through 1995. They do not provide a complete nonduplicative victim total.

case_name: Georgian and Ossetian displacement during the South Ossetia conflict, 1991–1992
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Ethnic Ossetians displaced from Georgia outside South Ossetia and ethnic Georgians displaced from South Ossetia to the rest of Georgia during and after the first conflict. The approximately 60,000 and perhaps 10,000 estimates describe distinct directional cohorts and are not added.
settlers: Georgian forces and South Ossetian separatist forces were the conflict parties named by the approved IIFFMCG passage. No distinct incoming settler population is established, and the approved locators do not provide a complete perpetrator roster or event-wide expulsion attribution.
source_labels: Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Conflict in Georgia, Report, Volume I (September 2009), printed pp.13–14 (physical PDF pp.14–15), paragraphs 5–6. Used only for the 1991–1992 fighting and June 1992 Sochi/JPKF institutional break. | International Crisis Group, South Ossetia: The Burden of Recognition, Europe Report No.205 (7 June 2010), report p.3 (physical PDF p.7). Used for the distinct approximately 60,000 Ossetian and perhaps 10,000 Georgian displacement estimates and later property/registration status; adjacent August 2008 figures are excluded.

case_name: Operation Osen phased deportation from Lithuania, September-November 1951
displaced: Lithuanian families classified as relatives or supporters of armed resistance and households categorized as kulaks. The reported 20,357 persons and approximately 4,000 kulak households are distinct units and are not added.
settlers: USSR and Lithuanian SSR security, party-administrative, local operational, rail and special-settlement authorities. This field records responsible actors, not an inferred incoming settler population.
source_labels: Lithuanian Genocide and Resistance Research Centre, Operation Osen documentary exhibit. Approved exhibit material supports the 5 September resolution and the 20–21 September, 2–3 October and 30 November phases, actors, categories, destinations and confiscation. The separately blocked dossier route is not used. | International Commission for the Evaluation of the Crimes of the Nazi and Soviet Occupation Regimes in Lithuania, conclusions, pp. 1–3, conclusions 2–10. Used as the institutional cross-check for Soviet deportation policy, affected categories and property removal.

case_name: M23-related North Kivu conflict displacement from March 2022, observed through 19 March 2024
displaced: Civilian residents displaced in North Kivu during the renewed M23 phase. Nearly 521,000 departures are attributed to an M23 offensive, as a nonunique, nonadditive movement estimate rather than an event-wide total.
settlers: M23 and FARDC-aligned forces are the principal belligerents in the bounded evidence. No distinct incoming settler population is established; MONUSCO is identified only as a protection and blocking-position actor.
source_labels: United Nations Secretary-General, Report on MONUSCO, S/2024/251 (21 March 2024), reporting period 1 December 2023–19 March 2024, paragraphs 19, 21–25 and 34–36. | UNHCR, ‘UNHCR warns of mounting needs in DR Congo as forced displacement continues’ (5 May 2023), opened body, with the source review’s M23-attributed count scope.

case_name: Bosnian Serb common plan to remove Muslims and Croats from claimed territory
displaced: Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats lawfully present in the twenty strategically important municipalities adjudicated in the Municipalities component. No nonduplicated event-wide number is established.
settlers: Bosnian Serb leadership and implementing political, military, police and municipal structures. This field identifies responsible actors; no distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Prosecutor v. Radovan Karadžić, Trial Judgment (24 March 2016), paragraphs 3435–3455, especially 3439–3447; printed pages 1294–1301, especially 1296–1298. Only this ICTY judgment was used for this case.

case_name: British annexation, phosphate-company settlement, and indentured migrant labour on Christmas Island
displaced: Indentured migrant phosphate workers identified by Parks Australia, including several hundred Chinese labourers; Malay and Sikh workers are also named. The evidence does not place every worker or every named population in one universal labor status.
settlers: British Crown authorities; John Murray and George Clunies-Ross as lessees; the Christmas Island Phosphate Company and British managers; and the imported labor communities involved in the phosphate settlement. Later operators belong to distinct phases.
source_labels: Parks Australia, Christmas Island National Park, ‘History’, Settlement and phosphate mining section. Used for the 1888 annexation and settlement, Crown lease and company, indentured migrant labour, British supervision, severe early conditions, community formation and attributed early Chinese-worker beriberi deaths. Only this Parks Australia page was used as the public source for this case.

case_name: French abandonment, reprisal, flight, transfer, and camp confinement of former Harkis and their families
displaced: Former Harkis and their families threatened by reprisals and moved from Algeria to metropolitan France. Other auxiliaries, officials, broader threatened-Algerian categories and the Pied-Noir exodus remain separate.
settlers: French military and ministerial authorities shaped disarmament, restricted transfer, transport and later reception. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Musée national de l’histoire de l’immigration, “1962,” section “La relégation des harkis”; François-Xavier Hautreux, “La guerre d’Algérie des harkis,” Les Chemins de la Mémoire no. 238 (September 2013), printed p. 3. Only these two institutional constituents of the existing compound identity were used for this case.

case_name: LURD–MODEL war displacement in Liberia, July 2000–2003
displaced: Liberian civilians displaced internally or across borders during the renewed war. Reported episodes and internal and refugee movements may overlap and do not establish a unique total.
settlers: Charles Taylor’s government, the Armed Forces of Liberia and aligned militias; LURD; and MODEL only on its distinct 2003 southeastern front. This field identifies responsible actors; no incoming settler population is established.
source_labels: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Liberia, Consolidated Final Report, Volume II, section 7.3.1, printed pages 134–136; section 7.4, printed pages 136–138; and section 9.1, printed pages 221–222. Only this TRC report was used for this citation. | Human Rights Watch, Back to the Brink: War Crimes by Liberian Government and Rebels (May 2002), physical and printed pages 2 and 7–8. Only this Human Rights Watch report was used for this citation.

case_name: Khmer Rouge urban evacuation and nationwide forced displacement in Cambodia, 1975–1979
displaced: Residents of Phnom Penh forced out beginning 17 April 1975; residents of other Cambodian cities and towns evacuated later during Khmer Rouge rule. Expelled foreign residents, internally displaced people and people who crossed into Thailand, Laos or Viet Nam remain distinct cohorts.
settlers: Khmer Rouge revolutionary forces and the Democratic Kampuchea regime carried out the evacuations. UNHCR attributes the broader campaign to Pol Pot; it does not establish a discrete evacuation order or a distinct incoming settler population.
source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, chapter 4, “Flight from Indochina,” printed pp. 91–92 (PDF physical pp. 13–14), with chapter endnotes 20–22 (PDF physical p. 26). Used only for the 17 April 1975 Phnom Penh emptying, later city and town evacuation, nationwide collectivized labour camps, internal displacement and separate 1975–1978 escape figures; later invasion flight and Thai border and camp phases are excluded.

case_name: Ruzizi Plain intercommunity-violence displacement in South Kivu, 1 December 2023–19 March 2024
displaced: Civilian residents of the Ruzizi Plain displaced by reported intercommunity violence. The source gives no displaced count, community-specific count, direction, destination or legal category.
settlers: The report discusses civilian vulnerability to armed-group violence along ethnic lines and separately names community groupings in Ruzizi tensions. It does not identify Ruzizi armed units, assign collective perpetration or establish an incoming settler population.
source_labels: United Nations Secretary-General, Report on the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, S/2024/251 (21 March 2024), introduction paragraph 1 and paragraphs 26–27, physical pages 1 and 5–6. Only this United Nations report was used for this bounded case.

case_name: Lachin capture and Azerbaijani civilian displacement, 17–18 May 1992
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Azerbaijani civilian residents of Lachin district, many of Kurdish descent. The approximately 30,000 estimate is attributed to Human Rights Watch as reproduced by the judgment and is approximate, nonadditive and not a household roster.
settlers: Forces of Armenian ethnicity captured Lachin. The parties disputed the degree of Armenian state-force participation. The judgment does not establish a distinct incoming settler population or a May 1992 land-transfer mechanism.
source_labels: European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, Chiragov and Others v. Armenia, application no. 13216/05, judgment (merits), 16 June 2015, paragraphs 12–30, 137–150, 169–186 and 192–208. Only this judgment was used for this bounded case.

case_name: Renewed armed conflict and civilian displacement in Kayah (Karenni) State from May 2021
dates: From May 2021; observed February 2022 and 28 March 2025, open end
displaced: Civilians and repeatedly displaced Kayah-origin families sheltering in forests, religious sites, communities, camps and neighboring southern Shan. “Karenni” identifies the state or region and does not assign one ethnicity to every displaced person.
settlers: The sources describe the Myanmar Armed Forces and opposing ethnic, local or other non-state armed groups. They do not provide a complete formation roster, incident-level perpetrator attribution or a distinct incoming settler population.
source_labels: UNHCR, “Displaced families in crisis-hit Myanmar struggle for survival” (21 February 2022), complete retained United Nations in Myanmar story body, especially the May 2021 onset and Demoso–Loikaw–southern Shan repeated-flight passages. | United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, Myanmar Humanitarian Update No. 45 (28 March 2025), physical pages 1–3, especially the southeastern Myanmar and Kayah displacement-condition passages.

case_name: Three Brotherhood Alliance offensive and civilian displacement in northern Shan from 26 October 2023
dates: From 26 October 2023; January 2024 ceasefire marker; observed through 28 March 2025, open end
displaced: Civilian residents of northern-Shan townships displaced to religious compounds, relatives and other sites, including people moving toward the China border. Separately, media reported crossings, whose exact numbers partners could not verify. Ethnicity, repeated-displacement status and a nonduplicated total remain unresolved.
settlers: The Three Brotherhood Alliance—MNDAA, TNLA and AA. The reported attacks targeted MAF and police bases, while reported fighting involved the MAF, EAOs and PDFs. This is not a complete later-phase roster. | No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, Myanmar: Escalation of clashes in northern Shan and the Northwest, Flash Update No. 3 (10 November 2023; as of 9 November), physical pages 1–2. | United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, Myanmar Humanitarian Update No. 45 (28 March 2025), physical pages 1 and 4.

case_name: Three Gorges Dam compulsory resettlement
displaced: Residents compulsorily relocated from Three Gorges reservoir inundation and project construction or relocation zones. Planned, estimated, audited and study-summary quantities remain separately attributed and nonadditive.
settlers: No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit. Receiving-area residents and relocated households are not reclassified as settlers.
source_labels: Michael M. Cernea, Hydropower Dams and Social Impacts: A Sociological Perspective, World Bank Environment Department Papers, Social Assessment Series 044 (January 1997), printed pp. 6, 21–22 (PDF pp. 12, 27–28). The Three Gorges figures are project estimates, not a verified final census.

case_name: Operation Vistula deportation and dispersal
displaced: People whom communist authorities defined as Ukrainian and removed from southeastern Poland, including Lemkos emphasized by the source | Cohort composition and unique-person totals remain unresolved; earlier border transfers and later returns are separate
settlers: Communist state, military and security authorities in Poland directed the removal and dispersed resettlement. | No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Andrzej A.
