Zięba, “Akcja ‘Wisła’: przyczyny i sprawcy, rezonans i konsekwencje” / “Operation ‘Vistula’: Causes and Perpetrators, Resonance and Consequences,” Rocznik Ruskiej Bursy 13 (2017), printed pp. 97–98, 115, 117, 126–127 (PDF pp. 1–2, 19, 21, 30–31). Causal and responsibility interpretations are attributed to the author.

case_name: Rwandan genocide, mass flight, and refugee return
displaced: Mainly Hutu civilians who crossed Rwanda’s borders in 1994, including refugees held under former-government and militia influence in camps | Rwandans internally displaced in 1994; this category remains separate from refugee stocks and return flows | Zairean Tutsi displaced from Masisi and earlier-1959 Tutsi refugees who moved to Rwanda in 1995–1996; these are distinct cohorts | Refugees moving west or returning to Rwanda during the 1994–1997 phases; repeated appearances across stocks and flows are unresolved

source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, “The Rwandan genocide and its aftermath,” chapter 10 of The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, printed pp. 245–273 (PDF physical pp. 1–29), with chapter endnotes at physical pp. 30–31. Stocks, flows and return estimates remain dated, attributed and nonadditive.

case_name: Partition of India and Pakistan and reciprocal mass displacement
displaced: Muslims who fled India for Pakistan in the source’s directional description | Hindus who fled Pakistan for India in the source’s directional description | People in smaller similar movements in succeeding years; no further quantity or terminal year is established
settlers: This source establishes reciprocal directional flight only. It does not establish incoming settler populations, rehabilitation or property reassignment for this public proposal.
source_labels: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, “Rupture in South Asia,” chapter 3 of The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: Fifty Years of Humanitarian Action, printed p. 3 / PDF physical p. 1; retrospective institutional account. The passage supports 1947, an attributed estimate of 14 million displaced, the stated Muslim and Hindu directions, and smaller succeeding-year movements only.

case_name: Burundi civil war and renewed mass displacement
displaced: Refugees who fled during the 1993 civil war, reported mainly in Tanzania | Civilians internally displaced at the crisis peak | Mainly Hutu civilians forced by the armed forces into regroupment camps during the later 1990s | People in spontaneous and organized return phases; repeated appearances across stocks, flows and returns are unresolved
settlers: The Burundian armed forces forced some mainly Hutu civilians into regroupment camps; rebel groups appear in the source as the stated security threat. | No incoming settler population, universal actor assignment or common receiving outcome is established for this event unit.
source_labels: Katherine Haver, Felicien Hatungimana and Vicky Tennant, Money matters: An evaluation of the use of cash grants in UNHCR’s voluntary repatriation and reintegration programme in Burundi, UNHCR PDES/2009/02 (July 2009), Context paragraphs 11–13 and footnote 8 at printed p. 4 / physical PDF p. 8; later return-program overview at printed p. 1 / physical PDF p. 5, paragraphs 1–2 only.

case_name: Armenian genocide deportations and forced removal
displaced: Armenian Christian people deported from northeastern border regions and, in later months, from almost all Ottoman provinces | People killed in local massacres or who died during deportation and in or en route to southern desert regions | Tens of thousands of Armenian children forcibly removed from their families; this is a separate cohort frame
settlers: The reviewed source establishes forced removal. It does not establish a distinct incoming settler population, property transfer or land redistribution for this bounded public account.
source_labels: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, “The Armenian Genocide (1915-16): Overview,” Holocaust Encyclopedia, last edited 7 November 2024. Used here only for spring 1915 through fall 1916, including the bounded actors, deportation geography, violence and separate attributed number frames stated on the page.

case_name: Solomon Islands Tensions displacement
displaced: Families from other islands evicted from Guadalcanal by the IFM, mainly Malaitan settlers and plantation workers | Mostly Guadalcanal families forced to abandon homes and live in the bush during later phases | People named in the TRC's forced-displacement testimony dataset; testimony, person and household frames are not a population total
settlers: Malaitan settlers and plantation workers appear in the source as a displaced cohort. The reviewed evidence does not support treating all displaced people as settlers or asserting a new incoming settler population for the event.

case_name: Nazi and Axis genocide of Roma and Sinti
displaced: European Roma and Sinti interned, deported or subjected to forced labor by Nazi German authorities | Roma shot or murdered in killing centers in German-occupied territories | Roma deported or killed by specifically identified allied or collaborating authorities; country and camp cohorts remain separate
settlers: The reviewed source establishes persecution, forced movement and killing. It does not establish a distinct incoming settler population, land transfer or settlement program for this bounded case.
source_labels: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, “Genocide of European Roma (Gypsies), 1939–1945,” Holocaust Encyclopedia, last edited 24 July 2023. Used here only for the bounded 1939–1945 Roma/Sinti case, locally attributed mechanisms, and separate uncertain number frames stated on the page.

case_name: Nicaragua post-2018 repression and exile
displaced: Nicaraguan students, human-rights defenders, journalists and farmers identified by UNHCR as continuing to flee | About 77,000 Nicaraguan refugees and asylum seekers hosted in Costa Rica in the 10 March 2020 snapshot; this was described as about two-thirds of the worldwide frame | Nicaraguan refugees and asylum seekers in Panama, Europe, Mexico and other countries within the same dated destination snapshot
settlers: The reviewed source establishes cross-border flight and asylum seeking. It does not establish a distinct incoming settler population, land transfer or settlement program for this bounded case.
source_labels: UNHCR, “Two years of political and social crisis in Nicaragua force more than 100,000 to flee,” briefing summary, 10 March 2020. Used here only for the April 2018 onset through that observation date, named cohorts and separate dated refugee/asylum-seeker frames; the observation date is not an endpoint.

case_name: Bougainville conflict displacement
dates: December 1988 escalation; conflict described as 1989–1997; peace marker in 1997
displaced: More than 20,000 civilians described as forced into government care centres in the 1989 operations frame | More than 5,000 displaced Bougainvilleans described as refugees in Solomon Islands through the 1997 peace marker; this may overlap other movement frames | Unquantified villagers and families who moved inland or into forest/BRA-controlled areas, plus separately described family movement to Australia
settlers: The reviewed testimony establishes conflict displacement. It does not establish a distinct incoming settler population, a quantified land transfer or an island-wide settlement program for this bounded case.
source_labels: Taloi Havini, presenting on behalf of Sister Lorraine Garasu, “Land and housing issues women have experienced in the conflict and post-conflict situation,” in Pacific regional consultation proceedings, printed pp. 141–153. Used only for the December 1988 escalation, 1989–1997 testimony frame, 1997 peace marker, and separately attributed movement cohorts and estimates.

case_name: Operation Sever deportations in the Baltic republics
displaced: Jehovah’s Witnesses and family members removed from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania; one study reports 475 people as 281, 44 and 150 national components | The Latvia frame reports 44 people, including six children under sixteen; the six are nested within 44 | The Estonian Commission reports an alternative Estonia estimate of 353 Jehovah’s Witnesses with family members, not additive to the study’s 281 Estonia component | The same study reports 283 former Anders Army members and family members deported from Lithuania under the separate Council resolution
settlers: The reviewed sources establish state deportation to special-settlement or exile destinations. They do not establish an incoming settler population or authorize a land-transfer claim for this bounded case.
source_labels: Estonian International Commission for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity, Phase III conclusions (2008), printed/PDF p. 9, section 8. Used only for the April 1951 Estonia frame and its alternative estimate. | Museum of the Occupation of Latvia, “TICĒT un KALPOT,” Operation North passage. Used only for the 31 March 1951 Latvia cohort and nested child count. | Elmar Gams, University of Tartu dissertation (2025), printed pp. 34–35 and 133. Used for the 31 March–1 April implementation, distinct authorization branches, tri-Baltic components and Lithuania-only Anders-family frame. | Institute of National Remembrance, 2nd Corps commemoration article, 20 May 2024. Used only for the same-night former 2nd Corps family branch and cohort-specific Irkutsk destination; its broad count is not equated with the Lithuania frame.

case_name: Land-law exclusion and migrant ejection in Tabou
displaced: Burkinabé migrants ejected from land in the article’s bounded Tabou example; no person, household or land-area quantity is given
settlers: The abstract discusses migrants, foreigners and descendants within land-law exclusion, but it does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this bounded ejection unit.
source_labels: Alfred Babo, “The Crisis of Public Policies in Côte d’Ivoire: Land Law and the Nationality Trap in Tabou’s Rural Communities,” English abstract. Used only for the 1998 Land Code, south-west plantation context, attributed nationality/autochthony framing and the Tabou example of Burkinabé migrants ejected from land.

case_name: Bulgarian assimilation campaign and forced migration of Turks
displaced: More than 340,000 people reported by Kutlay as forced to migrate from Bulgaria to Turkey by the end of August 1989 | Almost 40 percent, registered as 133,272, reported as later voluntary returns to Bulgaria; this is a nested outcome frame within the departure cohort, not an additional displacement count
settlers: The reviewed article establishes forced migration and later voluntary return. It does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this bounded case.
source_labels: Muzaffer Kutlay, “The Turks of Bulgaria: An Outlier Case of Forced Migration and Voluntary Return,” author-accepted manuscript, especially physical pp. 1–3 and 9–16. Used for the 1984–1989 campaign, more-than-340,000 departure frame and nested later-return frame.

case_name: Soviet deportations from Moldova
displaced: About 60,000 deportees attributed by the museum to the three operations collectively; this is an approximate combined frame, not a wave-by-wave or additive total
settlers: The reviewed source does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this bounded event.
source_labels: National Museum of History of Moldova, “Soviet Moldova: Between Myths and the Gulag.” Used only for the three nationwide deportation dates and the museum-attributed approximate combined frame of about 60,000 deportees.

case_name: Philippine–American War reconcentration
displaced: Villagers and rural populations confined in bounded protection zones under U.S. Army reconcentration orders; the reviewed source provides no population quantity
settlers: The reviewed source does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this bounded event.
source_labels: Christina Twomey, “Reconcentration and the Camp System: The Legacy of the Philippine-American War,” in Detention Camps in Asia (Brill, 2022), pp. 25–42; Monash abstract. Used only for the 1899–1902 orders, U.S. Army, villagers and rural populations, bounded protection zones, controlled movement, national Philippines frame, and source-attributed purpose.

case_name: Soviet deportation of the Kalmyks
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Nearly 120,000 as the article’s approximate overall deportation frame | 93,139 people in 26,359 families loaded on 46 trains in Beria’s separate reported frame; not additive to the overall estimate or destination allocations
settlers: The reviewed source does not establish a distinct incoming settler population for this bounded event.

Used for the dated deportation and return phases, differentiated Soviet roles, and attributed nonadditive population frames.

case_name: Isaaq civilian clearance in northern Somalia
displaced: At least one million people driven from their homes in HRW’s broad Somaliland war frame; uniqueness, stock-flow status, destinations, and an Isaaq-only or Hargeisa-only allocation are unresolved
settlers: HRW reports government repopulation of communities with civilians from other clans as Isaaq civilians fled; no settler count, universal scope, formal program, land-title transfer, or durable outcome is established
source_labels: Human Rights Watch, “Hostages to Peace”: Threats to Human Rights and Democracy in Somaliland (2009), “The Past as Prologue,” retained lines 438–461. Used for the 1988 Hargeisa bombing and strafing, Isaaq civilian flight and repopulation, broad attributed Somaliland war frames, and 1991 endpoint context.

case_name: Macías Nguema’s dictatorship and mass exile from Equatorial Guinea
displaced: Equatoguinean political opponents, intellectuals, officials, students and other residents driven abroad by repression and economic collapse; people already abroad and unable to return are a distinct cohort
settlers: No incoming settler population is established by the source
source_labels: Delmas Tsafack, “Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, and the management of Equatoguinean Refugees from 1960 to 1979,” Afrika Zamani 25 (2017), pp. 87–106, especially pp. 94–96 and 100–104. Complete article read; mediated scale estimates remain attributed and nonadditive.

case_name: Civil-war displacement within and from Sierra Leone
displaced: Sierra Leonean civilians repeatedly driven from homes and communities within the country and across borders, including into Guinea and Liberia
settlers: RUF as principal driver; AFRC, government forces and allied militias also committed violations; no incoming replacement population is established
source_labels: Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Witness to Truth, Volume Three A (2004), chapter 3, especially printed pp. 87 and 229 (physical PDF pp. 88 and 230). | Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Witness to Truth, Volume Three B, chapter 4, ‘Children and the Armed Conflict in Sierra Leone’ (2004), especially printed pp. 267, 308 and 315 (physical PDF pp. 35, 76 and 83). | Richard Conibere et al., Statistical Appendix to the Report of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone, Benetech Human Rights Data Analysis Group (2004), especially printed pp. 7–9 (physical PDF pp. 9–11). Non-random statement counts are not population totals.

case_name: ADF attack-driven displacement from Beni Territory and nearby Ituri villages, January–March 2021

case_name: Slavery, indenture and colonial residence in the Mascarenes and Seychelles
displaced: Enslaved Malagasy and African groups in specific island arrivals; Indian indentured workers in Mauritius, with differing recruitment, contract and residence histories. Not every traveller is shown to have been forced to depart.
settlers: Colonial authorities, traders and plantation owners shaped settlement and labour systems. Enslaved arrivals, contracted workers, former-worker landholders and returnee recruiters are distinct, possibly overlapping roles.
